name: PhanTap (Phantom Tap)
firmware_note: OpenWrt opkg package (not a full firmware image) that turns any two-port OpenWrt device into a transparent, MAC/IP-masquerading Linux bridge with an outbound OpenVPN pivot.
price_note: PhanTap itself is free, GPL-3.0 source. $25-30 is the retail price of the GL.iNet GL-AR150 router NCC Group built and tested it on; any two-Ethernet-port OpenWrt-capable device is claimed to work.
skill_note: Requires comfort with OpenWrt CLI, Linux bridging/netfilter, and OpenVPN to set up correctly; a misconfigured bridge is easy to make visible on the wire.
build_note: opkg install onto a stock OpenWrt build; no soldering, but the two-NIC bridge and VPN pivot need manual network configuration.
summary: PhanTap is an NCC Group red-team research project: an OpenWrt package that turns a cheap two-port router into an inline network implant which learns the victim device's MAC/IP and masquerades as it, so the implant is invisible to switches, NAC, and traffic monitoring, while phoning home over an OpenVPN tunnel on TCP/443 for remote pivoting. It was built and demonstrated on the GL.iNet GL-AR150 but is software, not a product.
honest_take: This is a research proof-of-concept, not a plug-and-play implant — you are building and hardening an OpenWrt bridge yourself, and the README itself flags real limits: the GL-AR150 caps out at 100Mbps against modern gigabit LANs, STP/pause/LACP frames aren't passed by a Linux bridge (so it can out itself on a switch that cares about those), and the victim's port stays 'live' even if the real device is unplugged, which is a detectable anomaly to anyone watching switch logs closely. NCC Group has not updated the core project's attack surface since 2019 even though the repo still gets maintenance commits; treat the NAC-bypass claim as solid 2019-era 802.1X, not a guarantee against modern posture-checking NAC.
best_for: Red team physical-access engagements against networks with basic 802.1X NAC
Learning how transparent-bridge MAC/IP masquerading defeats port-based NAC
Building a remote pivot point that survives a reboot of the tapped switch port
not_for: Gigabit networks (GL-AR150 hardware caps at 100Mbps)
Switches enforcing STP/LACP/pause-frame integrity checks
Anyone wanting a turnkey product — this is source code you assemble yourself
Covert ops where the victim's port going 'live-but-idle' after unplugging the real device would be noticed

hardware.mcu_primary_note: GL-AR150's SoC: single-core MIPS 24Kc @400MHz with integrated 2.4GHz 802.11n radio; PhanTap does not use the radio, wired-only implant
hardware.battery_note: No battery; powered via micro-USB or PoE depending on GL-AR150 variant
hardware.storage: 16MB flash + 64MB RAM on the reference GL-AR150; PhanTap package itself is a few hundred KB
notable_physical: Two Ethernet ports required for inline bridging
No external antenna needed since WiFi is unused

ethernet_mitm.note: Being an inline Linux bridge with SNAT to the victim's identity, it is positioned to inspect/alter traffic, though the stock package focuses on tunneling out rather than active injection

packet_capture.note: Full OpenWrt Linux networking stack; tcpdump available from the shell

cloud_c2.note: OpenVPN client tunnels out over TCP/443 to blend with HTTPS traffic and give the operator remote shell access

vpn_exfil.note: The OpenVPN pivot is the device's core exfil/access channel, documented in the README

usb_ethernet_attack.note: Not a USB gadget-mode device like a LAN Turtle or Packet Squirrel; it is a standalone inline router

usb_mass_storage.note: No USB gadget functionality at all

wifi_ap_mode.note: GL-AR150 has WiFi hardware but PhanTap's software does not use the radio

Physically installing an inline implant on a network you are not authorized to test is unauthorized access to a computer system in most jurisdictions (e.g. the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act), independent of how stealthy the implant is. Only deploy this against networks you own or have explicit written authorization to test.

name: Flipper Zero Add-On: Ethernet (ENC28J60)
firmware_note: Companion .fap app (ARP scan, LLDP passive discovery, ARP spoof, packet sniffer/PCAP export) installed via qFlipper/mobile app; not bundled in stock or Momentum firmware.
price_note: Board only; no Flipper Zero or RJ45 cable included.
skill_note: Plugs onto the Flipper's GPIO header and needs the .fap sideloaded, but using ARP scan/spoof/sniffer meaningfully requires basic network knowledge.
build_note: No soldering: clips onto the Flipper Zero's 18-pin GPIO header; install the app via GitHub release .fap file.
summary: A small GPIO daughterboard that gives the Flipper Zero a wired 10BASE-T Ethernet port via a Microchip ENC28J60 controller, paired with an open-source app for ARP scanning, passive LLDP discovery, ARP spoofing, and PCAP-exportable packet sniffing. It brings basic wired-network auditing to a device that otherwise has no Ethernet capability at all.
honest_take: The ENC28J60 is a 10Mbps-only, half/full-duplex 10BASE-T chip from the 2000s — it will not see or touch a modern gigabit-only switch port, and even where it links up, throughput is a fraction of what a $10 USB Ethernet dongle on a laptop gives you. The real value is convenience (it rides on hardware you already carry) rather than raw capability; a Raspberry Pi Zero with the same ENC28J60-class chip and Ettercap will out-perform it for actual MITM work. ARP spoofing on a network you don't control and don't have permission to test is illegal in most places even though the app makes it a two-tap operation.
best_for: Quick ARP/LLDP recon on a wired network segment you're authorized to test
Pulling PCAPs off a LAN drop for later analysis in Wireshark
Learning basic wired-network reconnaissance on hardware you already own
not_for: Gigabit Ethernet (10BASE-T only)
High-throughput packet capture or sustained MITM sessions
Networks you don't have explicit authorization to test

radios.note: 10BASE-T half/full duplex only, SPI bus up to 20MHz, 8KB on-chip packet buffer

ethernet_tap_passive.note: LLDP passive discovery listens without sending probes; ARP scanner is active

name: Int3rcept0r
price_note: Estimated parts cost: Raspberry Pi Zero (~$10-15), ENC28J60 Ethernet shield (~$5-8), jumpers and microSD not included in listed price.
skill_note: Requires flashing Raspbian, editing boot config for SPI/USB gadget mode, wiring GPIO jumpers, and configuring Ettercap/DNSMASQ/iptables by hand.
build_note: No assembled option; buyer sources a Pi Zero + ENC28J60 shield and follows the GitHub setup script.
summary: A homebrew LAN Turtle-equivalent built from a Raspberry Pi Zero using g_ether USB gadget mode to appear as a USB-to-Ethernet adapter, bridging a victim's Ethernet connection to the attacker's USB host while running Ettercap-based ARP/DNS spoofing and credential sniffing (Telnet, FTP, POP3, SSH1, SMB, MySQL, HTTP) with reverse SSH/Netcat/Meterpreter backdoors for remote access.
honest_take: This is functionally a DIY clone of Hak5's LAN Turtle, built from parts that cost a fraction of the $50 Hak5 device — but you're trading that savings for hours of manual Raspbian/iptables/Ettercap configuration and none of the polished module marketplace or support the commercial product has. The credential-sniffing module only catches cleartext protocols (Telnet, FTP, POP3, SSH1, unencrypted HTTP); against a modern network running TLS and SSH2 everywhere, the 'credential theft' headline feature mostly nets nothing. Development stopped in April 2024 after 9 commits, so treat it as a proof-of-concept to learn from rather than a maintained tool.
best_for: Learning how g_ether USB gadget mode enables an inline network MITM device
Budget-constrained labs studying ARP/DNS spoofing mechanics
Understanding the LAN Turtle attack class before buying the commercial product
not_for: Networks using TLS/SSH2 for everything (the cleartext-protocol sniffer catches nothing)
Anyone wanting vendor support or a module ecosystem
Production red-team engagements needing a maintained, supported tool

name: PoisonTap
price_note: Cost of a bare Raspberry Pi Zero plus a microSD card; the project itself is free open-source code.
skill_note: Setup is scripted, but understanding and safely wielding the DNS-rebinding/cache-poisoning attack chain requires real web-security depth.
build_note: Flash Raspbian, drop in the PoisonTap scripts, configure isc-dhcp-server/dsniff/Node.js, reboot — no assembled product exists.
summary: Samy Kamkar's 2016 proof-of-concept: a Raspberry Pi Zero that emulates a USB Ethernet adapter when plugged into a locked or unlocked computer, tricks the OS into routing all traffic through it via a DHCP response claiming the entire IPv4 space, then siphons HTTP cookies across the Alexa top 1M domains through hidden iframes and force-caches persistent WebSocket backdoors in the browser cache — all without needing to unlock the screen.
honest_take: This is the direct ancestor of the O.MG Cable / Packet Squirrel class of device already in this database, and it's worth understanding for that lineage alone, but it does essentially nothing against a fully modern browser: any cookie with the Secure flag survives, any site with HSTS blocks the HTTP downgrade the whole attack depends on, and both are now close to universal on major sites. It is not a keystroke injector (a common mix-up with Rubber Ducky-class devices) — PoisonTap never types anything, it hijacks network routing and browser caching. The GitHub repo has been dormant since 2018 with 90 open issues and no license file, so there's no vendor and no update path; it survives purely as a teaching example.
best_for: Understanding DNS-rebinding and browser cache-poisoning attack chains
Demonstrating why HSTS and the cookie Secure flag matter to non-technical audiences
Historical/educational study of the LAN-Turtle/O.MG-Cable device lineage
not_for: Attacking any site that enforces HSTS or sets Secure on its cookies (most major sites today)
Keystroke injection or payload execution — it has none
Anyone wanting a maintained or supported tool

name: RPi0 USB-A Addon Board
price_note: A near-identical 4-pogo-pin USB-A addon board (same 'Responder or PoisonTap type attacks' marketing copy) is sold directly from China as the REES52 'Raspberry Pi Zero W/Zero USB-A Addon Board' for roughly Rs.309 (~$3.70), and again under other brand names (ZeroKey, Geekworm BadUSB addon). Hacker Warehouse's $6 price is a reseller markup on what appears to be a generic, widely cloned design, not a unique product.
skill_note: Screws onto the Pi Zero's pogo pins; no soldering, but reviewers note the mounting screws need firm installation.
build_note: Pogo-pin connector board; screws onto a Raspberry Pi Zero to add a full-size USB-A host port.
summary: A $6 pogo-pin breakout board that gives a Raspberry Pi Zero (not included) a standard full-size USB-A port, marketed specifically for running Responder or building PoisonTap-style USB implants that otherwise need a micro-USB-to-USB-A adapter cable. Four spring-loaded pogo pins engage the Pi Zero's USB data/power test points on the underside of the board.
honest_take: This is purely a physical connector — there is no silicon on it, no logic, and it does nothing by itself. It exists to save you from carrying a flaky micro-USB OTG adapter cable when building a Pi Zero implant. The entire capability of whatever you build comes from the software running on the attached Pi Zero (PoisonTap, Responder, Int3rcept0r, etc.), not from this board. It also isn't a Hacker Warehouse original: the identical 4-pogo-pin design and near-word-for-word 'Responder or PoisonTap type attacks' marketing copy shows up under at least three other brand names (REES52, ZeroKey, Geekworm) at a fraction of the price directly from overseas suppliers — you're paying roughly a 60% markup here for US-based stock and a matched screw-down fit, not for any unique engineering.
best_for: Builders assembling a Pi Zero-based USB implant who want a solid USB-A port instead of an adapter cable
PoisonTap or Responder-style projects specifically
not_for: Any use as a standalone tool — it has zero function without a Pi Zero and matching software
Anyone expecting logic, storage, or protection circuitry on the board

name: WiebeTech Forensic ComboDock v5
skill_note: Straightforward to operate (choose write-block or read/write mode at power-on) but chain-of-custody discipline matters for the results to hold up.
build_note: Desktop dock; connect a bare drive, plug in cables, power on and pick a mode from the menu.
summary: A desktop forensic drive dock that forces an explicit write-blocked-or-read/write choice every time it powers on, so a forgotten mode setting can't silently let an examiner write to evidence media. It bridges SATA and Ultra ATA (IDE) drives out to FireWire 400/800, USB 3.0, and eSATA host interfaces.
honest_take: CRU/WiebeTech's ComboDock family has a real NIST CFTT track record — NIST/DHS published hardware write-block test reports for the original 'WiebeTech Forensic ComboDock' (USB and FireWire interfaces) in 2006, and for 'WiebeTech Forensic ComboDock v6' in 2022 (Federated Testing) — but the exact revision sold here as 'v5' does not have its own dedicated NIST CFTT report in the record I could locate; the closest documented version is a 'v5.5' SKU referenced in reseller catalogs. Treat any 'this exact box is NIST-validated' claim as unverified for the v5 specifically, even though the ComboDock architecture as a family has a solid CFTT history. The vendor's own listing here makes no explicit court-admissibility or NIST claim at all — that language shows up in third-party CFTT test reports, not the product page.
best_for: Imaging SATA or IDE evidence drives with a guaranteed, mode-selected write block
Labs that also need occasional FireWire or eSATA drive access on the same dock
Chain-of-custody workflows requiring an explicit human choice of mode at every power-on
not_for: NVMe or M.2 drives (SATA/IDE only)
Anyone needing a specific, individually NIST CFTT-certified serial/revision without checking CRU/WiebeTech directly for this exact unit's test status
Modern high-speed forensic imaging where USB-C/Thunderbolt speeds matter (this dock tops out at USB 3.0/FireWire 800)

hardware.case: Metal/plastic desktop enclosure with LED mode indicator and menu system

usb_mass_storage.note: In read/write mode, a docked drive mounts as normal mass storage over the USB 3.0 interface

standalone_untethered.note: Requires a host computer connected via one of its interfaces to be useful; it does not image or operate independently

legal.notes: Standard, legal forensic lab equipment. A write-blocker does not itself create legal risk; improper evidence handling procedures around it can undermine admissibility, which is a chain-of-custody/procedure issue rather than a hardware one.

name: WiebeTech Drive eRazer
skill_note: LCD-menu driven, no computer needed; picking the wrong erase mode for your compliance needs is the main user risk.
build_note: Standalone appliance: connect a bare SATA or IDE drive, select an erase mode from the LCD menu, run.
summary: A standalone appliance that wipes bare SATA (2.5"/3.5") and PATA/IDE 3.5" drives (with 1.8" ZIF/IDE adapters) at native interface speed without a computer, claiming roughly 7GB/min on modern drives and 2GB/min on older ones, with an LCD menu of preconfigured erase modes and automatic label printing support.
honest_take: The Hacker Warehouse listing for this base 'Drive eRazer' model does not name a specific wipe standard (no DoD 5220.22-M or NIST 800-88 language on that page) — those named standards (DoD SANITIZE, NIST 800-88 Clear/Purge, 12 erase modes) are documented for CRU's higher-end 'Drive eRazer Ultra' model, a different, later product. Don't assume this base model meets a specific compliance standard unless CRU's own datasheet for this exact model says so; if a specific certification matters for your audit trail, verify directly with CRU/WiebeTech before relying on it. Also: no wipe, from any vendor, defeats a drive-level SSD wear-leveling reserve — for SSDs, ATA Secure Erase or the drive's own sanitize command is generally the more defensible method, and this appliance's marketing doesn't distinguish HDD from SSD behavior.
best_for: Bulk, computer-free decommissioning of SATA/IDE spinning hard drives
IT asset disposal workflows wanting a standalone, no-laptop-required eraser
Labs already using WiebeTech ComboDock hardware wanting a matching eraser appliance
not_for: Compliance workflows that specifically require a documented DoD 5220.22-M or NIST 800-88 Purge/Clear certification on the exact model used — confirm with CRU rather than assuming this base model qualifies
SSDs and NVMe drives, where wear-leveling can leave data recoverable after this kind of overwrite pass
Anyone needing network-attached or unattended bulk wiping of many drives simultaneously

name: Rainbow Tables HDD
skill_note: Using the tables requires separate cracking software (e.g. RainbowCrack, Ophcrack, or coWPAtty/cowpatty-format tools); none is confirmed included.
summary: A 2TB USB 3.0 external hard drive preloaded with precomputed rainbow/lookup tables for cracking A5/1 (GSM voice encryption), LM hashes, WPA-PSK (1 million words across 1000 preselected SSIDs), and two MD5 variants. The drive itself is generic storage; the only product here is the dataset that's already copied onto it.
honest_take: This is a generic 2TB USB drive plus files that have been freely downloadable for over a decade — the WPA-PSK set matches the well-known Church of WiFi tables (172,000-1,000,000 words x 1000 SSIDs, originally distributed as 7-33GB torrents by RenderLab since the 2000s). You're mostly paying $190 to skip the download and get it on a drive already, which is a real convenience but not a unique dataset. The WPA-PSK tables only work if your target's SSID happens to be one of the 1000 baked in — because WPA-PSK's key derivation salts with the SSID, a rainbow table only pays off per-SSID, so this is close to useless against an uncommon or custom network name. For WPA cracking specifically, modern practice has largely moved to GPU-accelerated hashcat brute-forcing and PMKID attacks rather than precomputed tables, and A5/1 rainbow tables target 2G GSM voice/SMS, a niche and largely superseded attack surface today.
best_for: Historical/educational cracking demos against known, common SSID names
Labs wanting a ready-to-go copy of long-established public rainbow table sets without downloading tens of GB
not_for: Cracking WPA-PSK on any network whose SSID isn't one of the 1000 baked into the table

name: BusKill
price_note: Cable-only ranges $59-79 depending on connector (USB-A/USB-C); the full Kit (cable + companion app setup) is $99-119.
skill_note: Basic screen-lock/shutdown triggers are point-and-click through the companion app; the LUKS self-destruct trigger requires hand-editing udev rules and shell scripts on Linux.
build_note: No assembly for the hardware itself (a magnetic breakaway USB extension); install the companion app for Windows/macOS/Linux to configure triggers.
summary: A laptop dead-man's switch: a USB extension cable interrupted by a strong magnetic breakaway connector that clips to your body. The cable itself is dumb hardware with no chip — all detection and response logic runs as software on the laptop, watching for that specific USB device's removal and firing a configured trigger (lock screen, shutdown by default; an optional, off-by-default script can shred a Linux LUKS header).
honest_take: There's no electronics in the BusKill cable at all — it's a magnetic USB breakaway connector, and the 'smarts' are entirely the open-source buskill-app watching for that specific device to disappear. The LUKS self-destruct feature that shows up in most coverage of this device is NOT included by default and not what you get by just buying the cable: BusKill's own docs state plainly it 'will not be released with this self-destruct trigger' — you have to write your own udev rule and script to wire it up, Linux-only, and it is irreversible (no pre-made backup of the LUKS header means permanent data loss, including from an accidental trip). The plain lock/shutdown triggers are reliable and low-risk; the self-destruct trigger people associate with the product name is a DIY add-on with real failure modes of its own (SSD wear-leveling can leave key material behind despite an overwrite, and an accidental snag destroys everything with no recovery).
best_for: Journalists, activists, and travelers wanting a quick screen-lock/shutdown trigger if a laptop is snatched or seized
Linux users comfortable writing their own udev rule who want an evidence-destruction failsafe and understand the irreversibility
Anyone wanting an actively maintained, fully open-source (GPL-3.0) triggering app across Windows/macOS/Linux
not_for: Anyone expecting the LUKS wipe out of the box — it requires manual setup and is Linux-only
Situations where a false-positive trigger (bumping the cable) would be catastrophic, given the self-destruct option's irreversibility
Non-Linux systems if a self-destruct rather than lock/shutdown is the goal

hardware.mcu_primary_note: No microcontroller; the cable is a passive magnetic breakaway USB extension. All logic runs as host-side software (buskill-app) that detects the specific paired USB device's removal.

summary: A fully open-source inline hardware keylogger for QWERTY keyboards that stores roughly 3 million characters in onboard flash and is retrieved over a hidden Wi-Fi network at up to ~30m range, with vendor-claimed support for remote keystroke injection back into the host. It's part of the RedBulletTooling KEYVILBOARD family, which also includes an SMS-exfiltration variant on the same open hardware base.
honest_take: Unlike most hardware keyloggers in this category, KEYVILBOARD is genuinely open-source top to bottom (firmware and hardware on GitHub under MIT), which is a real differentiator from closed competitors like KeyGrabber — you can audit exactly what it does with captured keystrokes instead of trusting a vendor's word. That said, 'remote key injection' is a vendor claim on the Tindie listing that I could not independently verify against the firmware source in the time available, so treat it as claimed rather than confirmed. Like all inline hardware keyloggers, it doesn't require drivers or show up as a new process to antivirus software — but that's true of every device in this category, not a special feature of this one; the real detection risk is physical (a technician spotting an extra inline module) or, on some designs, an unexpected USB hub/device enumeration, which the vendor doesn't address either way here.

name: Ovrdrive USB
price_note: Crowd Supply campaign launched at a $69 early price; $79 reflects the batch's recorded price. Campaign shipped ("Ovrdrive USB - Shipped!" update on Crowd Supply).
skill_note: Normal hidden-data use just needs a specific triple-reinsertion sequence, but enabling the physical self-destruct requires cutting a PCB trace — an irreversible hardware modification.
build_note: Ships assembled and ready to use in its default "Lite" mode; the self-destruct circuit requires the user to physically cut a trace on the PCB to arm, which counts as a soldering-adjacent modification.
summary: An open-hardware 16GB USB flash drive (ATtiny24A logic MCU + SM3257ENT flash controller) that reads as blank/broken unless plugged in three times in quick succession, at which point the real 16GB partition mounts normally. A separate, disabled-by-default circuit can invert the flash chip's supply voltage to heat it past 100°C as a physical self-destruct, armed only by cutting a PCB trace.
honest_take: Multiple independent outlets (PCBWay's own engineering write-up, Hackster.io, CNX Software, TechSpot) describe a 16GB flash chip (part K9HDG08U1A), which contradicts the 8GB figure in some early coverage — treat 16GB as the better-sourced number for the shipped product, though an earlier prototype may genuinely have used 8GB. The self-destruct feature that gets all the headlines is disabled out of the box and requires physically cutting a trace to enable — most buyers who never do that are just getting a USB drive with a mildly clever hidden-partition trick, not a self-destructing one. Interrupt Labs themselves note the voltage-inversion heating may not be hot enough alone to fully destroy the NAND without an added thermite-like compound, so even 'armed' units aren't a guaranteed data-destruction method without further DIY work. This is squarely an anti-forensics tool for journalists/researchers in hostile environments, and using the self-destruct feature against data under a legal hold or active investigation carries real legal exposure regardless of the underlying data's content.

not_for: Anyone wanting a guaranteed, one-step self-destruct — it's off by default and needs an irreversible hardware mod to enable, and even then may not fully destroy the chip without added modification
Concealing data from a forensic examiner who images the raw flash rather than relying on the OS-visible partition table
Anyone who might need to defeat a legal hold or ongoing investigation — see legal notes

name: O.MG Malicious Cable Detector
price_note: Hak5's own shop lists $40 direct from the vendor. EU/UK resellers charge more: Lab401 ~€69 (~$74.52), KSEC Worldwide ~£56.95. Also seen at $60 across storefronts.
skill_note: Plug the cable into the detector, then the detector into a USB port; LED indicates the result. No configuration required for basic use.
build_note: Ready to use out of the box; Arduino-IDE-compatible firmware and a 6-pin ISP header allow advanced users to modify it.
summary: A small bus-powered inline dongle that samples a connected USB-A cable's power draw 200,000 times per second, using side-channel power analysis to flag cables with hidden active electronics (like O.MG-style implant cables) that stay electrically invisible on the data lines until triggered. It doubles as a USB data blocker ("USB condom") for safe charging.
honest_take: O.MG's own product description admits the limit plainly: it 'is not a guarantee against bespoke nation-state-grade implants, but it covers the commercially available malicious cables' — this is a signature/power-fingerprint check against known classes of implant, not a cryptographic or exhaustive guarantee. There's also a timing gap inherent to the method: because implant cables like O.MG's own products are designed to stay dormant until remotely triggered or a specific condition is met, a clean reading only means 'not actively transmitting data during this test,' not 'verified safe.' That's the single most common misread of what a green light here means. As a data blocker alone it's solid and simple — charge-only USB condoms are a mature, low-risk category — but buying it purely for the detector half and expecting certainty against a sophisticated implant overstates what side-channel power sampling can promise.
best_for: Quick screening of found or borrowed USB-A cables against known malicious-cable power signatures
Safe charging from untrusted public USB ports (data-blocker function)
Security-aware travelers and pentesters wanting a lightweight, purpose-built screening tool
not_for: Guaranteed detection of custom or nation-state-grade cable implants, per the vendor's own disclaimer
USB-C cables (compatibility stated as USB-A only)
Detecting an implant that stays fully dormant for the entire test window

summary: KeyGrabber is Keelog's long-running hardware keylogger line, sold at Hacker Warehouse across three variants: PS/2 (4MB), USB Pico (16MB), and USB WiFi Premium (16MB, timestamping, Mac compatibility, wireless retrieval). name: Masterkey - WiFi USB Keylogger
price_note: Seller marked "On A Break" and not accepting orders as of research date.
skill_note: Plug-and-play for basic logging, but writing Ducky Script injection payloads and using the Live Execute feature needs real scripting familiarity.
build_note: Fully assembled, plug-and-play; firmware is open source and re-flashable over-the-air if you want to modify it.
summary: An inline USB pass-through keylogger built around an ATmega32U4 (USB HID passthrough to the keyboard/host) and an ESP8266 (WiFi retrieval), running a modified fork of spacehuhn's wifi_keylogger project. It logs keystrokes to the ESP8266's filesystem, serves a web interface over its own "Masterkey" access point at 192.168.4.1, and can also run Ducky Script keystroke-injection payloads live or from saved scripts — combining keylogging and HID injection in one device, from the ESP32 Marauder author.
honest_take: This is honestly closer to 'an ESP8266 plus an ATmega32U4 in a 3D-printed case, running a fork of a well-known open-source project' than a from-scratch design — the vendor's own listing credits spacehuhn's wifi_keylogger as the base, which is fair and transparent, but worth knowing if you'd rather build the equivalent yourself for the cost of the two chips. The default AP password is documented in the wild (open-source repo), so if you deploy one, change the Wi-Fi credentials immediately or anyone in range who knows the project can pull your logs. It's one of the only devices in this batch that combines logging AND scripted HID injection in a single $45 device, which is a genuine capability edge over pure loggers like KeyGrabber or the generic extension-cable keylogger — but the GitHub repo (justcallmekoko/USBKeylogger) hasn't been pushed to since March 2021, so treat it as a frozen, unmaintained snapshot rather than an actively supported tool.

name: EvilCrow-Keylogger
vendor: Joel Serna & Ernesto Sánchez; PCB manufactured and distributed by April Brother
skill_note: Plug-and-play for basic logging; the ATmega32U4 and ESP32-PICO firmware can be re-flashed by the user for custom builds.
build_note: Comes pre-flashed and ready to use; two jumpers are included specifically for users who want to reflash the ESP32.
summary: An open-hardware inline USB keylogger combining an ATmega32U4 (native-USB HID device to the target PC, driven via the Arduino Lilypad USB bootloader) with a MAX3421E USB host controller to read the attached keyboard, an ESP32-PICO for WiFi log access, and a microSD slot for onboard backup logging. Sold via multiple regional resellers (AliExpress, Tindie, EU/UK/Mexico distributors) with fully open firmware and hardware design (CC-BY-4.0).
honest_take: This is a genuine dual-USB-role design — MAX3421E reads the physical keyboard on the device's host port, and the ATmega32U4's own native USB (with the Lilypad bootloader specifically used for HID emulation) re-presents those keystrokes to the downstream target PC — so the 'inline passthrough' framing in reseller listings checks out against the actual hardware, unlike some competitors that leave this ambiguous. It logs and forwards; it does not inject scripted payloads or emulate an independent HID attack device the way the Masterkey does, so don't buy this expecting Rubber-Ducky-style scripting. The GitHub README is upfront that 'some keys or modifiers have not been implemented' across the 11 supported keyboard layouts — expect occasional dropped or misread keys, especially with less common layouts, rather than a flawless capture rate. Actively maintained (pushed January 2026) which is unusual for this category — most competitors here are dormant.
